parts.partTitle: JDK vs JRE vs JVM & How Bytecode Runs Fast

beats.headline: JDK, JRE, JVM — stop guessing which one to install.
beats.subline: They aren't competing downloads. They're nested layers built for Write Once, Run Anywhere.
beats.narration: Every Java setup guide throws three acronyms at you: JVM, JRE, and JDK. They aren't rival downloads—they're nested layers, and once you see how they stack, Java setup clicks.

beats.title: The 3 Nested Layers of Java
beats.subtitle: Always install a JDK — it bundles everything

nodes.label: JVM (Java Virtual Machine)
nodes.detail: Class Loader, Bytecode Verifier, Execution Engine, JIT & GC

nodes.label: JRE (Java Runtime Environment)
nodes.detail: JVM + Standard Class Libraries (String, List, HashMap, I/O)

nodes.label: JDK (Java Development Kit)
nodes.detail: Adds dev tools: javac compiler, javap, jar, javadoc & jdb

beats.narration: At the core sits the JVM, which verifies bytecode, executes it, and runs garbage collection. Wrap it with standard libraries like List and HashMap, and you get the JRE. Add javac and dev tools on top—that's the JDK. Always install a JDK.

beats.title: Inside a .class File (0xCAFEBABE)
beats.caption: javac outputs portable stack-based bytecode

lines.text: 0: iload_1   // push int 'a' onto operand stack
1: iload_2   // push int 'b' onto operand stack
2: iadd      // pop both, add, push sum

beats.narration: When javac compiles your code, it builds platform-neutral bytecode stamped with hex CAFEBABE—if that signature is missing, the JVM throws ClassFormatError. Run javap dash c and you'll see clean stack instructions like iload, iadd, and ireturn.

beats.title: Why HotSpot Java Isn't Slow
beats.subtitle: Tiered Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation at runtime

nodes.label: Interpreter
nodes.detail: Starts executing bytecode instantly for fast startup

nodes.label: C1 JIT Compiler
nodes.detail: Compiles warm, frequent methods to quick native code

nodes.label: C2 JIT Compiler
nodes.detail: Heavy optimizations: inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis

beats.narration: So why isn't bytecode slow? HotSpot starts by interpreting cold code for snappy startup. Once a method gets busy, the C1 JIT compiles it to native code, and C2 aggressively optimizes hot paths with inlining and loop unrolling.

beats.title: Mental Model Locked In
takeaways: JDK = JRE + compiler tools (always install a JDK)
0xCAFEBABE bytecode runs on any OS with a JVM
HotSpot C1 & C2 JIT compile hot paths to native speed

parts.partTitle: Installing Java 21 LTS & Fixing PATH / JAVA_HOME

beats.headline: 'javac' is not recognized — before line 1 of code.
beats.subline: Here's how to install a clean Java 21 LTS and wire up PATH & JAVA_HOME right the first time.
beats.narration: Nothing kills day-one momentum faster than seeing javac is not recognized in your terminal. Let's pick the right Java 21 LTS build and fix the two environment variables behind almost every setup bug.

beats.title: Which JDK Should You Install?

top.label: 6-Month Feature Releases
points: Replaced every 6 months — not ideal as a baseline

bottom.label: OpenJDK Java 21 LTS (or 25 LTS)
points: Years of free security patches & ecosystem support

beats.narration: Java ships free, open-source builds under OpenJDK. Grab Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, or Azul Zulu—and pick a Long-Term Support release. Java 21 LTS is the industry baseline right now, with Java 25 as the next LTS.

beats.title: Fast Install & Version Check
beats.caption: SDKMAN on macOS/Linux, winget on Windows

lines.text: # Open a NEW terminal & verify both match

beats.narration: On macOS or Linux, use SDKMAN to install Temurin 21 and switch versions effortlessly. On Windows, run winget or the Adoptium MSI with Add to PATH checked. Then open a fresh terminal—both java and javac dash version should match.

beats.title: PATH vs. JAVA_HOME (The #1 Trap)

top.label: PATH (For Your Shell)
points: Lets your terminal find java & javac
Debug mismatches with: where java / which java

bottom.label: JAVA_HOME (For Maven, Gradle & IDEs)
bottom.code:
✅ C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21
❌ C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21\bin
points: Tools append bin/javac onto JAVA_HOME themselves

beats.narration: Here's the classic trap. PATH needs the JDK's bin folder so your shell finds javac. JAVA_HOME is checked by Maven, Gradle, and IDEs, and must point to the JDK root—never bin, or tools search for bin slash bin slash javac.

beats.title: JDK 21 Wired Up Cleanly
takeaways: Install Java 21 LTS (Temurin, Corretto, or Zulu)
PATH points to /bin; JAVA_HOME points to JDK root
Always open a brand-new terminal after env edits
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): CLI javac/java, single-file launch & IntelliJ vs Eclipse →
beats.narration: If java works but javac fails, check where java or which java for an old JRE ahead in PATH. In Part 3, we compile from the CLI and set up IntelliJ and Eclipse.

parts.partTitle: CLI javac/java, Single-File Launch & IntelliJ vs Eclipse

beats.headline: Docker containers don't have an IDE Play button.
beats.subline: Master javac and java in 30 seconds, then level up with IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse.
beats.narration: If IntelliJ compiles code with one click, why bother with the terminal? Because when a CI build breaks or a Docker container won't boot, there's no green Play button—only javac and java.

beats.title: Your First File & IDE Shortcuts

steps.explanation: Filename MUST match the public class name with exact capitalization: HelloWorld.java.
In IntelliJ: type 'main' + Tab for main(), 'sout' + Tab for println, and click the gutter to set a red breakpoint.

beats.narration: Start with HelloWorld dot java—make sure the filename matches your public class capitalization exactly. Inside IntelliJ, typing main plus Tab expands the whole method, sout plus Tab prints a line, and clicking the gutter drops a breakpoint.

beats.title: CLI Compile, Run & Single-File Launch
beats.caption: Pass the class name, NEVER .class — or launch .java directly
beats.narration: From the terminal, run javac HelloWorld dot java to generate HelloWorld dot class, then run java HelloWorld—never pass dot class or it fails. Need a quick test? Since Java 11, java HelloWorld dot java compiles and runs straight in memory.

beats.title: IntelliJ IDEA vs. Eclipse IDE

top.label: IntelliJ IDEA Community (Recommended)
points: Clean layout: src/ for code, out/ for .class, skip .idea/ in Git
Auto-detects or downloads JDK 21 (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S to change)
Run (Shift+F10) & visual debugger (F8 Over, F7 Into, F9 Resume)

bottom.label: Eclipse IDE for Java Developers
points: Workspace holds multiple projects; compiles on save into bin/
Point Installed JREs → Standard VM to your JDK 21 root folder
Debug Perspective: F6 Step Over, F5 Step Into, F8 Resume

beats.narration: For real projects, pick IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition—it's free, compiles src into out, and even downloads JDK 21 for you. Prefer Eclipse? Point Installed JREs to your JDK 21 root, and it compiles on every save into bin.

beats.title: Environment Ready! Run the Lab
takeaways: javac compiles to .class; java takes class name (no .class)
java File.java runs single files in memory for quick tests
Use IDE breakpoints to inspect variables line by line
